tls-handshake.alt: A browser and a website set up TLS in four steps. First the browser says hello and lists what it supports. Second the website replies with its certificate. Third the browser checks the certificate: a trusted issuer, the right name and still valid. Fourth the two sides agree on session keys. After that, everything is encrypted with those keys.
tls-handshake.caption: The certificate proves which server this is. The key exchange gives both sides the same session keys without sending them.

In a full tunnel, both work traffic and web traffic travel through the encrypted tunnel to the company, and web traffic then goes out to the internet from there. In a split tunnel, only work traffic uses the tunnel and everything else goes straight from your device to the internet.

zero-trust.alt: A Zero Trust layout in two parts. In the data plane, a subject sends a request to a Policy Enforcement Point that stands in front of the resource. The enforcement point asks the Policy Decision Point in the control plane. The decision point weighs who is asking, whether the device is healthy and whether the context fits, then returns allow or deny. Only then is the request let through, for that session only.
zero-trust.caption: The decision point decides, using identity, device and context. The enforcement point stands in the path and carries the decision out, one request at a time.

digital-signature.alt: Signing: the sender hashes the message to get a digest, then signs the digest with their private key. The message and signature travel together. Checking: anyone hashes the received message to get digest A, and uses the sender's public key on the signature to get digest B. If A equals B, the message was not changed and only the sender's private key could have made the signature.
digital-signature.caption: Signing uses the private key; checking uses the public key. A match gives integrity, proof of origin and non-repudiation.

key-exchange.alt: A paint-mixing picture of key exchange. Alice and Bob start from a public colour that anyone can see. Each mixes in a secret colour of their own and they swap the mixtures in the open. Each then adds their own secret colour again to the mixture they received. Both end with the same final colour, the shared secret. Someone listening saw the public colour and both mixtures, but cannot un-mix them to get that final colour.
key-exchange.caption: Diffie-Hellman in paint: two people agree on a shared secret over an open channel without ever sending the secret itself.

sql-injection.alt: A sign-in form where the username field contains admin, a quote mark and two dashes. The app pastes that text straight into its database query. The quote ends the name early and the two dashes turn the rest, the password check, into a comment. The attacker is signed in as admin with no password. The fix is parameterized queries, which always treat input as data and never as code.
sql-injection.caption: Injection works when input is pasted into a command. The attacker's text stops being data and becomes part of the instruction.

email-auth.alt: A message claiming to be from bank.example arrives at your mail server. Your server looks up bank.example's DNS records and asks three things. SPF: is the sending server on the list allowed to send for this domain? DKIM: does the message's signature match the domain's public key? DMARC: if either check fails, should the message be delivered, quarantined or rejected, and where should a report go? Messages that pass go to the inbox; failures are quarantined or rejected.
email-auth.caption: SPF is the guest list, DKIM is the wax seal, and DMARC is the domain owner's rule for what to do when either one fails.

sso-federation.alt: You sign in once at an identity provider with your password and multifactor authentication. The identity provider then sends each application, here email, an HR app and a partner's site in another organization, a signed statement saying who you are. Each app trusts that statement, so no app ever sees your password. When that trust crosses organizations it is called federation.
sso-federation.caption: Single sign-on: authenticate once, and the identity provider vouches for you to every app. Federation extends that trust to other organizations.

oauth-pkce.alt: The OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE in six steps. One, the app asks the authorization server to sign the person in and sends a hash of a secret it just made, the code challenge. Two, the person signs in and approves what the app may do. Three, the authorization server sends a short-lived code to the registered redirect URI. Four, the app sends the code together with the secret itself, the code verifier, and the server checks it matches the hash from step one. Five, the server returns an access token, and with OpenID Connect an ID token too. Six, the app calls the API with the access token. A stolen code is useless without the secret verifier.
oauth-pkce.caption: PKCE ties the code to the app that started the flow. Only that app knows the secret behind the hash it sent at the start.

risk-matrix.alt: A three by three grid. Likelihood runs up the side from low to high and impact runs across from low to high. Cells toward the top right are high risk, cells toward the bottom left are low risk and the diagonal between is medium. Example A, a phished admin password, is likely and very harmful, so it sits in the top right and is treated first. Example B, the lobby display going offline, is unlikely and minor, so it sits in the bottom left and is reasonable to accept.
risk-matrix.caption: Risk is likelihood and impact together. The matrix turns a long list of worries into an order for dealing with them.
